questions.stem: You are managing a project that moves a hospital's ward medicines from nurse-held stock to pharmacy-dispensed patient packs. Training sessions are booked for next month. Ward nurses are asking their managers why the change is happening at all, and a rumour says it is really about cutting nursing posts. The chief pharmacist sponsors the project but has so far left all communication to the project team. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Add a section on the patient-safety reasons for the change to the start of each training session, so every nurse hears the case from the trainers.
options.rationale: The candidate puts the 'why' in the right content but the wrong mouth and the wrong moment. Trainers cannot answer the staffing rumour with any authority, and by the time training starts the rumour has had another month to settle.

options.text: Ask the chief pharmacist to explain the reasons for the change to ward nurses in person, at briefings held before the training begins.
options.rationale: The reason for a change, and anything touching jobs, carries weight only from the person accountable for the decision. Nurses who hear it from the sponsor before training arrive at the sessions knowing why they are there.

options.text: Publish a detailed question-and-answer page on the intranet from the project team that addresses the staffing rumour and sets out the clinical benefits.
options.rationale: A project team page treats the problem as missing information rather than missing leadership. A denial of job cuts from the project team is not credible, because the project team does not decide staffing.

options.text: Ask the ward managers to reassure their nurses at handover that no posts are affected, and to collect any further questions for the project team.
options.rationale: Line managers are a good channel, but the candidate asks them to give an assurance they have no authority to give and may not be able to stand behind. The message that matters most still has no owner.

questions.explanation: People judge a change by who stands behind it. The case for a change, and any statement about its effect on jobs, needs to come from the sponsor who owns the decision, and it needs to arrive before people are asked to learn the new way of working. Project teams, trainers and line managers can repeat and explain that message, but they cannot substitute for it.
questions.mindset: The reason for a change is the sponsor's to give, and it should be heard before the training starts.

questions.stem: Your project is introducing a new structural design-checking tool at an engineering consultancy where junior engineers rarely question senior colleagues. Training sessions mix grades, and each ends with an open question slot that nobody uses. The post-training survey, which senior engineers gather from their own teams, reports no issues. Yet in the first fortnight of the trial, checks done by junior engineers show three times the expected error rate. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Extend the standard training course by a further half day for every grade, concentrating on the parts of the tool where the trial errors have occurred so far.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes the cause is a knowledge gap without confirming it, and repeats the mixed-grade format that has already suppressed every question. More of the same session will produce more of the same silence.

options.text: Ask the senior engineers to review every check made by their junior colleagues in the tool until the trial error rate falls back to the expected level.
options.rationale: Extra review contains the errors but does nothing to explain them, and it routes the problem through the same hierarchy that is hiding it. Juniors are even less likely to admit difficulty to the person now checking their work.

options.text: Hold short follow-up sessions for junior engineers without senior colleagues present, and add an anonymous route for reporting difficulties with the tool.
options.rationale: The culture is filtering out the very information the project needs. Removing the seniors from the room and offering an anonymous route lets juniors say what they are struggling with, so the cause of the errors can be found rather than guessed.

options.text: Report the survey result and the trial error rate to the sponsor, and recommend that the rollout pauses until the cause of the errors is understood.
options.rationale: Pausing may become sensible, but the candidate escalates before doing the inexpensive work of finding out why. The project can collect better information within days without stopping anything.

questions.explanation: Feedback channels are shaped by the culture they run through. Where people do not challenge those above them, open questions in mixed groups and surveys gathered by managers will report calm while performance data says otherwise. When the data and the feedback disagree, trust the data and change the channel so the people closest to the problem can speak safely, before deciding what the fix is.
questions.mindset: When performance and feedback disagree, suspect the channel before concluding the feedback is true.

questions.stem: You are leading the introduction of a labour-scheduling system at a distribution centre in the Netherlands. It will move warehouse staff from fixed shifts to demand-based shifts published a week ahead. The company's agreement with its works council requires the council's advice before any change to working patterns. Go-live is in four weeks; the council next meets in six. The operations director says the system is only a tool and the council need not be involved. What should you do?

options.text: Ask HR to put the change to the works council for advice now, requesting an extra meeting if needed, and replan go-live around the outcome.
options.rationale: The change to working patterns is exactly what the agreement covers, whatever the system is called. Starting the advice process at once through the people who hold the council relationship protects the go-live as far as it can be protected, and the plan follows the obligation.

options.text: Accept the operations director's view, since he owns warehouse operations, and record his decision and the reasoning behind it in the project decision log.
options.rationale: The candidate treats a binding agreement as a matter of operational judgement. Recording the decision documents the breach rather than preventing it, and a challenge from the council could halt the rollout after go-live.

options.text: Brief the works council chair informally on the new system this week, so the council is aware of it before go-live without a formal advice request.
options.rationale: Awareness is not advice. The candidate seeks a softer route that feels collaborative but does not satisfy the agreement, and it may leave the chair feeling the council was managed rather than consulted.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor that the operations director disagrees with involving the council, and ask the sponsor to rule on whether advice is required.
options.rationale: Escalation suits a genuine disagreement about discretion, but there is no discretion here. The candidate invites a senior manager to decide whether to honour an agreement the company has already made, and loses time doing so.

questions.explanation: Where an organisation has a formal agreement with employee representatives, any change within its scope triggers the agreed process, however the project describes the change. A change to how people work is assessed by its effect on them, not by whether it arrives as software. The project manager's job is to start the required process early, through whoever owns that relationship, and plan around it, not to look for a way past it.
questions.mindset: Judge whether a change triggers a people obligation by what it does to people, not by what the project calls it.

questions.stem: A county council is rolling out a new purchasing process in three waves. Wave one went well, largely because the finance director who sponsored it spoke at every site briefing. She has now moved to another authority. Her successor says he supports the change but is busy with budget setting and has not yet engaged. Wave two, covering the sceptical highways and waste depots, starts in three weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the former finance director to record a short video endorsing the new process, to be shown at the wave two briefings in place of a sponsor appearance.
options.rationale: The candidate keeps the form of the sponsorship without its substance. Sceptical depots are watching whether current leadership cares, and an endorsement from someone who has left signals the opposite.

options.text: Start wave two on the planned date and ask the wave one site managers to vouch for the new process when they meet their colleagues in the depots.
options.rationale: Peer advocacy is a useful supplement, but the candidate substitutes it for authority. Depots that are already doubtful will read the new sponsor's absence as a sign that the change has lost its backing.

options.text: Meet the new sponsor this week to explain the part his predecessor played and agree the specific visible actions he will take before wave two begins.
options.rationale: Visible sponsorship was a cause of wave one's success, and the most sceptical sites are next. Three weeks is enough to secure it if the conversation happens now, and a busy sponsor commits more readily to a few named actions than to a general role.

options.text: Postpone wave two until budget setting has ended and the new sponsor has the time to take an active part in the depot briefings himself.
options.rationale: Postponing might become necessary, but the candidate concedes before asking. Nobody has yet told the new sponsor what is needed from him, and a delay costs momentum the first wave earned.

questions.explanation: A change in sponsor mid-change resets one of the main reasons people adopt it, and the risk is greatest just before the most resistant groups are reached. Treat a sponsor handover as something to complete deliberately: brief the newcomer on what sponsorship has involved, agree concrete visible acts, and do it while there is still time to adjust the plan. Substitutes for sponsorship rarely carry the same signal.
questions.mindset: When the sponsor changes, re-establish sponsorship before the next group of people is asked to change.

questions.stem: An online retailer has moved six teams to persistent product teams that report progress against quarterly outcomes. The executive committee's monthly review still asks each team for a Gantt chart and percentage complete, and each team spends about a day a month producing them. The teams want you, as delivery lead, to tell the committee the old report is no longer meaningful. The committee chair has said she does not yet trust the outcome measures. What should you do?

options.text: Replace the Gantt reports with the outcome measures from next month, with a short note to the committee explaining why the old figures mislead them.
options.rationale: The argument may be right, but the candidate removes information leaders rely on against the chair's stated position. A governance body that loses its familiar view before it trusts the new one tends to ask for more reporting, not less.

options.text: Keep supplying the old report for now, show the outcome measures alongside it, and agree with the chair which old figures can be dropped as her confidence grows.
options.rationale: The chair has said exactly what is missing: trust in the new measures. Running both for a time lets her test the outcome measures against the figures she relies on, and agreeing the retirement of each old figure with her moves the change at the pace confidence allows.

options.text: Have one analyst produce all six Gantt reports centrally from the team boards, so the teams recover their time while the committee still receives what it asked for.
options.rationale: This solves the cost and quietly abandons the change. The candidate makes the old report cheaper to sustain, so nothing ever prompts the committee to move to the measures the teams are actually managed by.

options.text: Ask the chair to sponsor a workshop where the committee and team leads design a new review format together to replace the current monthly report.
options.rationale: Co-design is attractive, but it asks the committee to design away its reporting before it believes the alternative. The candidate addresses the format when the chair has named confidence in the measures as the obstacle.

questions.explanation: Changing how leaders see progress is an organisational change in its own right, and it moves at the speed of their trust in the new information. Running old and new views side by side for a period, and retiring old measures one at a time by agreement, costs some duplication but builds the evidence the new measures need. Removing the familiar view first, or making it cheap enough to keep for ever, both stall the change.
questions.mindset: Retire an old measure when the people who rely on it trust its replacement, and help them get there.

questions.stem: Your agile team ships an update every two weeks to the scheduling app used by 900 home-care workers. Recent updates have moved buttons and renamed screens, and care coordinators report that workers are phoning the office to ask how to do tasks they did easily a month ago. The product owner points out that each change was requested by users and tested well in reviews. What should you recommend?

options.text: Keep deploying fortnightly, but hold changes to workers' screens behind feature flags and release them together on a predictable date with brief guidance.
options.rationale: Separating deployment from release keeps the team's rhythm while giving workers a pace they can absorb. The trade-off is that some finished work waits weeks to reach users, which is a smaller cost than a workforce relearning the app every fortnight.

options.text: Slow the team's delivery cadence to one release a quarter, so that every change reaches workers in a single larger update they can learn at once.
options.rationale: The candidate fixes a user-facing problem by giving up the team's fast feedback and steady flow. How often the team deploys and how often workers see change are separate decisions, and only the second is causing the trouble.

options.text: Add a short in-app tour to each fortnightly update that shows workers what has moved, so they can find features without phoning the office.
options.rationale: A tour eases each change but leaves the frequency untouched. The candidate treats the burden as a discovery problem when it is the rate of relearning, and care workers between visits have little time for tours.

options.text: Ask the care coordinators to brief their workers on each update at the weekly team meeting, using release notes written by the product owner.
options.rationale: The candidate moves the cost of change onto coordinators who are already absorbing the phone calls, and the workers still face a new layout every two weeks. It manages the symptom while keeping its cause.

questions.explanation: Users have a limited capacity to absorb change, and each improvement draws on it even when the improvement is good. In iterative delivery the team's deployment cadence and the users' release cadence can be set separately: keep the first fast for learning and quality, and set the second at a rhythm the people affected can absorb, with support timed to it. Bundling user-visible change costs some speed to value in exchange for adoption.
questions.mindset: Deliver at the team's pace but release at the pace the people affected can absorb.

questions.stem: Your agile team at an insurer has delivered four new features to the claims assessment tool this quarter, each meeting the definition of done. Usage data shows assessors have barely touched three of them, and team leaders say they did not know the features existed or how they changed the assessment procedure. The product owner asks how to stop this happening with the features planned for next quarter. What should you suggest?

options.text: Add a separate communication sprint at the end of each quarter in which the team prepares guidance and briefings for every feature delivered in it.
options.rationale: The candidate recognises that change work is needed but batches it away from the features, so assessors hear about a feature up to three months after it arrives. Change work delayed is value delayed.

options.text: Ask the training department to run a refresher course for assessors each quarter that covers every new feature added to the tool during the period.
options.rationale: This hands the change to a group outside the team, on a quarterly cycle, and still leaves the written assessment procedure out of date. The candidate treats readiness as training rather than as part of finishing the feature.

options.text: Extend the definition of done for features that alter how assessors work, so the procedure update and a team leader briefing are finished before the item counts as done.
options.rationale: If the procedure and the people who run it have not changed, the feature has not delivered its value. Putting that work in the definition of done makes it visible, sized and completed alongside the code.

options.text: Send release notes to all assessors and team leaders on the day each feature is deployed, with a link to a short video showing how the new functionality is used on a live claim.
options.rationale: Release notes create awareness at best and are easily ignored. The candidate informs people about software without changing the procedure that tells them how to assess a claim.

questions.explanation: A feature that changes how people work is not finished until the way they work has changed with it. Agile teams make that explicit by treating the operational change, such as updated procedures and briefed team leaders, as part of the work item and its definition of done, so it is planned and delivered at the same pace as the software instead of trailing behind it.
questions.mindset: Count the change to how people work as part of the work, not as something that follows it.

questions.stem: A building society's pilot agile team halved its mortgage-product lead time in nine months. The chief operating officer now wants the pilot team's exact practices written up as a standard playbook and mandated for twelve more teams from next quarter, with compliance checked monthly. The pilot team's coach has been asked to write the playbook. As the transformation lead, what should you do?

options.text: Write the playbook as asked, but include a section on which practices each team may adapt, so the twelve teams can tailor it within the monthly compliance checks.
options.rationale: Adding flexibility softens the mandate but keeps its assumption that the practices are what produced the result. Monthly compliance checks will still pull teams towards following the document rather than learning from their own work.

options.text: Roll the playbook out to three of the twelve teams first, and use their first quarter's results to decide whether to extend it to the other nine teams.
options.rationale: Phasing reduces exposure and sounds evidence-based, but it tests the wrong thing. The candidate accepts that copying practices is the method and only questions how fast to do it.

options.text: Agree to the playbook and monthly checks, and ask the COO to fund an external coach for each new team so the practices are adopted faithfully from day one.
options.rationale: Coaching helps, but the candidate points it at faithful copying. Twelve coaches enforcing one team's practices on different work is an expensive way to get the form of the pilot without its learning.

options.text: Explain to the COO that the gains came from how the pilot team learned, and propose placing pilot members in the new teams to help each one adapt the practices.
options.rationale: The pilot's result came from a team inspecting and improving its own way of working. Spreading the people who did that, rather than a snapshot of where they ended up, carries the capability that produced the gain.

questions.explanation: Practices that worked for one team are the output of that team's learning in its own context, not a recipe that carries the result with it. Scaling a change in ways of working means spreading the capability to learn and adapt, usually through people who have done it, rather than mandating the final form of one team's process and auditing compliance with it.
questions.mindset: Spread the ability that produced a result rather than a copy of the result.

questions.stem: An aircraft maintenance company is replacing paper task cards with tablets, using fixed hangar go-live dates and agile software teams. In user testing, night-shift engineers object strongly to the new design, which drops the free-text margin where they used to write notes. The day-shift supervisor says the night shift simply dislikes change and the margin was never an approved field. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Spend time with the night shift to find out what the margin notes were used for, then have the product owner decide how the new design meets that need.
options.rationale: Strong objection to losing an informal practice often means the practice is doing a job nobody designed for, such as passing information between shifts. Finding out what it does lets the product owner meet the need properly.

options.text: Ask the product owner to restore a free-text notes field on the tablet, since the users' objection is strong and the field costs little to build.
options.rationale: The candidate responds to the strength of the objection without understanding it. Rebuilding an unapproved field may carry an uncontrolled record into a regulated system and may still miss the real need behind it.

options.text: Confirm with the quality manager that margin notes are not an approved record, and if so explain to the night shift why the field is being removed from the design.
options.rationale: This settles whether the notes are allowed, not what they were doing. If they carried essential information between shifts, removing them with an explanation removes that information too.

options.text: Arrange extra coaching for the night shift on the new tablet workflow, since their objection has arisen before they have used it on live work.
options.rationale: The candidate accepts the supervisor's reading that this is dislike of change and treats it as a skills gap. Coaching people to work without something they may genuinely need does not make the need go away.

questions.explanation: Resistance is information before it is a problem. When a group objects to losing something that was never formally part of the process, the informal practice is often carrying real work, and a new system that removes it can break something nobody listed in the requirements. Find out what the practice does before deciding whether to keep it, replace it or retire it.
questions.mindset: Treat strong resistance as a clue to a need the design has missed until you know otherwise.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is moving a university's departments to a self-service purchasing system in which staff buy low-value items directly against a budget. Department administrators used to approve every purchase and now lose that step. Two months in, several administrators are quietly telling staff to keep sending paper requests to them 'for now'. The rollout plan, which you own, gives administrators no role. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the sponsor to issue an instruction that paper purchase requests will no longer be accepted after a set date, and communicate the date to every department.
options.rationale: A deadline may be needed eventually, but the candidate uses authority to close the workaround while leaving its cause untouched. Administrators who have lost their role will find another way to stay in the loop.

options.text: Withdraw the paper request forms from the intranet and have the finance office return any paper request it receives to the member of staff who sent it.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the problem as a channel to be shut. Staff are caught between the system and their administrator, and the administrators are given further reason to see the project as working against them.

options.text: Report the administrators' advice to staff as non-compliance to the heads of department concerned, and ask them to address it through normal line management.
options.rationale: The candidate treats a predictable reaction to losing a role as misconduct. Pushing it into line management hardens the resistance and alienates the people best placed to make the new process work locally.

options.text: Redesign the remaining rollout so administrators lead it in their own departments and receive the new monthly spending reports, giving them a defined place in the process.
options.rationale: The workaround is a response to lost standing, and the rollout plan is the project manager's to change. Giving administrators a real role, leading adoption and overseeing spend, turns the people closest to staff into advocates rather than blockers.

questions.explanation: Changes that remove part of someone's role, especially an approval or gatekeeping step, threaten their standing as well as their routine, and the usual response is quiet workarounds rather than open objection. The durable fix is to design a new role for the people affected inside the change, which is often within the project manager's own authority over the rollout. Enforcement alone closes the workaround but keeps the reason for it.
questions.mindset: When a change takes something from people, give them a place in what replaces it.

questions.stem: A housing association is introducing a new repairs-booking process for its 60 trades operatives. HR has nominated six change champions, chosen because they are newer staff with lighter workloads. In early sessions, experienced operatives ignore the champions' advice and ask their foremen instead. Two foremen are well respected and used the new process in the pilot, but taking them off the tools for champion work will delay some repairs. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the six nominated champions and give them extra training on the new process, so that they can answer the operatives' questions with more confidence and authority.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes the champions lack knowledge, when what they lack is standing with experienced peers. More training does not give newer staff the credibility that the operatives are looking for.

options.text: Agree with the repairs manager to release the two foremen part-time as champions, accepting some repair delay, and pair each of them with existing champions.
options.rationale: Champions work through peer credibility, and the operatives have already shown whose advice they trust. Some repair delay is a real cost, but it buys the adoption the whole process change depends on, and pairing develops the newer champions too.

options.text: Ask the foremen to answer questions informally when operatives come to them, while the nominated champions continue to run the formal champion sessions.
options.rationale: This avoids the repair delay by relying on goodwill. The foremen's support stays unplanned and unrecognised, and the formal network remains built around people the operatives do not listen to.

options.text: Replace the champion sessions with a recorded video walkthrough of the new process that operatives can watch at the depot in their own time.
options.rationale: The candidate removes the people problem by removing the people. Experienced operatives were asking someone they trust, and a video answers neither their specific questions nor their doubts.

questions.explanation: Change champions are effective because of who they are to their peers, not because they have time to spare. Selecting them for availability rather than credibility is a common false economy. Releasing respected practitioners costs operational capacity, and that cost is usually worth paying because adoption depends on whose word people trust.
questions.mindset: Choose change champions for the trust they hold, and pay the price of their time.

questions.stem: A shared services centre is automating invoice matching, which will remove much of the manual work done by its 45 accounts payable clerks. Decisions about future roles will not be made until the automation has been tested in four months. Since a vague announcement last month, rumours of redundancies have spread and two experienced clerks have resigned. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask the sponsor and HR to tell staff now what has been decided, what has not, and when role decisions will be made.
options.rationale: Uncertainty is easier to live with than a vacuum. Stating plainly what is known, what is not and when it will be known removes the space rumours fill, and it comes from the people who own the role decisions.

options.text: Involve experienced clerks in testing the automation and designing how exceptions will be handled in the new process.
options.rationale: The clerks understand the exceptions the automation will struggle with, and taking part gives them influence over what happens rather than having it done to them. It is useful to the project and to the people affected.

options.text: Tell the clerks that the project does not expect any redundancies, so the team is steadier while the automation is tested.
options.rationale: The candidate offers reassurance the project manager has no authority to give and that the facts may not support. If roles are later reduced, every other message from the project loses its credibility.

options.text: Hold all further communication about the automation until role decisions are made, so staff receive one complete and accurate message.
options.rationale: Waiting for a complete message sounds careful, but four months of silence after a vague announcement is exactly what is feeding the rumours. The candidate trades accuracy for timeliness and loses more staff in the gap.

options.text: Bring forward the automation go-live date to shorten the period of uncertainty for the clerks and limit any further resignations.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the length of uncertainty as the problem rather than how it is handled. Rushing testing to shorten it raises delivery risk while doing nothing about what staff are being told.

questions.explanation: When a change affects jobs and the decisions are not yet made, silence is read as bad news. The honest response is to say what is known, what is not and when it will be, through the people who own the decisions, and to give those affected a real part in shaping the change. Reassurance beyond the facts and waiting for a perfect message both damage trust more than the uncertainty itself.
questions.mindset: Say what you know and when you will know more, because silence is heard as the worst case.

questions.stem: Your agile team has launched a self-service portal for a travel company's customers to change their bookings. Uptake is far below forecast. You find that call-centre team leaders are measured on calls handled per agent, and some are telling customers who mention the portal that a call is quicker. The contact centre director sets those measures. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Show the contact centre director the portal data alongside the call-handling measures, and ask whether the measures should change.
options.rationale: The team leaders are responding rationally to how they are measured. The person who sets the measures is the one who can remove the conflict, and seeing the two sets of figures together lets the director decide with the evidence.

options.text: Invite call-centre team leaders to sprint reviews and use their knowledge of difficult booking changes to shape the next portal features.
options.rationale: Team leaders know which changes customers find hard and why they call. Involving them improves the product and gives them a stake in the portal succeeding rather than a reason to compete with it.

options.text: Remove the option to change bookings by phone for simple changes, so that customers are directed to use the portal instead.
options.rationale: The candidate forces adoption by removing choice, a decision that belongs to the business rather than the delivery team. It also leaves team leaders measured on a volume the company now wants to fall.

options.text: Raise the team leaders' behaviour with their line managers as a breach of the company's digital strategy, and ask for it to stop.
options.rationale: The candidate treats a response to incentives as misconduct. Even if the behaviour stops, the measure that caused it is still in place and will produce the next workaround.

options.text: Add a prominent banner on the booking website promoting the portal as the fastest way to change a booking, to raise uptake directly.
options.rationale: Promotion addresses awareness, but the customers in question already knew about the portal and were talked out of it. The candidate works on the wrong cause.

questions.explanation: People do what they are measured and rewarded for, so a change that conflicts with existing performance measures will be resisted by people acting entirely reasonably. The fix lies with whoever owns the measures, and the project's part is to make the conflict visible to them with evidence. Involving the affected group in shaping the change turns competitors into contributors.
questions.mindset: When people resist a change, check what they are rewarded for before questioning their attitude.

questions.stem: Your firm is introducing the same new stores-ordering process at three client organisations with very different cultures. Match each organisation to the change approach most likely to work there. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A retail cooperative where significant changes are decided by elected member representatives at regional forums.
A franchise network where each store is owned and run as an independent business by its franchisee.
A rail maintenance contractor where work is done only to approved written procedures that staff are audited against.

options.text: Design the process with a working group of member representatives and take it to the forums for decision
options.rationale: In a cooperative, legitimacy comes from the members' own decision-making. A process shaped by their representatives and approved at the forums carries authority that no management instruction would.

options.text: Pilot it in a few stores and have those owners present the cost and time results to their peers
options.rationale: Franchisees are business owners, not employees, and adopt what makes commercial sense. Evidence from peers running the same kind of business is the most persuasive case that can be put to them.

options.text: Issue it as a revised controlled procedure, with competency sign-off before staff use it
options.rationale: In a procedure-governed organisation, a change is real only when the controlled procedure changes. Until then staff are audited against the old one and are right to keep following it.

options.text: Announce it through a chief executive instruction with a single go-live date for every site
options.rationale: Not used. Franchisees cannot be instructed in this way, a cooperative would see it as bypassing its members, and in the procedure-driven contractor an instruction does not change the procedure staff are audited against.

questions.explanation: The same change needs a different route into different organisations, and the route is set by where legitimacy and authority sit in each culture. Before choosing how to introduce a change, ask who people regard as entitled to change how they work: members, owners, controlled documents or managers. A route that ignores that answer is resisted however good the change is.
questions.mindset: Introduce a change through whatever the organisation already treats as legitimate authority.

questions.stem: A water utility is rolling out a new mobile work-scheduling system to its field engineers. Match each situation to the person best placed to handle it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: An engineer privately asks whether the new scheduling rules will change her standby allowance and her childcare arrangements.
Engineers at one depot want someone who has used the system on real jobs to show them the shortcuts.
The network and customer-service directorates each insist the scheduling rules follow their own priorities, and sign-off is blocked.

options.text: Her line manager
options.rationale: Personal impact on pay and working arrangements is a conversation for the person who manages the individual, who knows her circumstances and can involve HR. It should not be handled in a group setting or by the project.

options.text: A super-user from the pilot depot
options.rationale: Practical know-how from real jobs is what super-users offer. A peer who has done the work answers 'how do I actually do this' more credibly than a trainer or manager.

options.text: The project sponsor
options.rationale: A conflict between directorates over priorities sits above both of them and above the project manager. Resolving it is a core sponsor duty, because only the sponsor's authority spans the two.

options.text: The system vendor's trainer
options.rationale: Not used. A vendor trainer knows the system's features but not the utility's allowances, its depots' working practice or its internal priorities, which is what each situation turns on.

questions.explanation: Different roles carry different kinds of authority in a change. Line managers handle what a change means for an individual, peer super-users handle how to do the work, and the sponsor resolves conflicts that cross organisational lines. Sending each concern to the role that can actually answer it is faster and more credible than routing everything through the project.
questions.mindset: Send each change concern to the role whose authority actually answers it.

questions.stem: A media company's agile transformation is now colliding with older organisational systems. Complete each sentence with the response that fits best. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Funding is still allocated each year to fixed-scope projects, so product owners must raise a change request to reorder their own backlog. The transformation lead should
Appraisals still rank individuals on personal output, and developers have started avoiding pairing and code review. The transformation lead should

options.text: propose to the finance director a two-quarter trial of funding one product team by capacity rather than by scope
options.rationale: The funding model belongs to finance and it is what forces the change requests. A bounded trial lets the owner of the model see how capacity funding works before being asked to change it more widely.

options.text: take the evidence on pairing to the HR lead who owns appraisals and propose team-based objectives
options.rationale: The appraisal system is rewarding the opposite of the collaboration the transformation needs. HR owns it, and evidence of the behaviour it is producing is what makes the case for changing it.

options.text: advise developers to treat the appraisal criteria as secondary until HR updates them
options.rationale: Not used. It asks developers to take a personal career risk on the transformation's behalf, while nobody who owns the appraisal system is told there is a conflict.

options.text: ask product owners to keep raising change requests until the funding model is formally reviewed
options.rationale: Not used. It accepts the collision as permanent and makes the teams carry its cost, with no date or owner for the review it waits for.

questions.explanation: A change to how teams work runs into every organisational system built for the old way: funding, appraisal, approval and reporting. Those systems have owners outside the project, and they rarely change unless someone shows them, with evidence, what the conflict is costing. Leaving teams to work around the conflict hides it from the people who could remove it.
questions.mindset: Take a conflict between new ways of working and old systems to the people who own the old systems.

questions.stem: A rail infrastructure company must train 340 track engineers on a new inspection procedure before it replaces the old one. Each course lasts 6 hours and takes up to 12 engineers. Past rollouts suggest 15% will need a further 3-hour coached session. Engineers in training are backfilled at €48 per hour. Work out the figures the change budget needs.

blanks.label: Number of 6-hour courses needed
blanks.rationale: 340 ÷ 12 = 28.33, and a part-filled course still has to run, so 29 courses are needed. Rounding down would leave four engineers untrained.

blanks.label: Total engineer hours spent in training, including coached sessions
blanks.rationale: Courses: 340 × 6 = 2,040 hours. Coached sessions: 15% of 340 = 51 engineers × 3 = 153 hours. Total 2,040 + 153 = 2,193 hours.

blanks.label: Backfill cost, in €
blanks.rationale: 2,193 hours × €48 = €105,264. This is the operational cost of releasing people to learn, and it belongs in the change budget alongside the cost of the courses.

questions.explanation: The cost of an organisational change includes the time people spend away from their work to learn it, not just the cost of delivering training. Sizing it means counting everyone affected, allowing for those who will need more support, and pricing the cover required while they are away. Budgets that omit backfill push the cost onto operations, which then protects itself by releasing fewer people.
questions.mindset: Price the time people need to change, because unfunded time is time that will not be released.

questions.stem: A law firm replaced its document management system three months ago. Fee earners have stopped arguing that the old system was better. They are now trying shortcuts, building their own folder templates and asking many 'how do I…' questions, and productivity is starting to recover. The diagram shows the stages of a change curve, each with the response suited to it. Select the stage the firm has reached.

graphic.title: Four stages of a change curve, each labelled with a suited project response
graphic.caption: Select a stage. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between stages, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Denial: repeat the reasons for the change and what it means for each person
regions.rationale: Denial shows as people carrying on as before and treating the change as something that will pass. These fee earners are actively using the new system, so they are well beyond this stage.

regions.label: Resistance: listen to concerns and fix the genuine problems raised
regions.rationale: Shortcuts can look like workarounds, which tempts a reading of resistance. But the arguing has stopped and the shortcuts are being built inside the new system, which marks the move past this stage.

regions.label: Exploration: give practical support such as quick guides and floor-walkers
regions.rationale: Experimenting, building personal templates and asking how to do things are the signs of exploration. People have accepted the change and are working out how to make it work, so practical help is what they need.

regions.label: Commitment: recognise success and hand over to business as usual
regions.rationale: Recovering productivity can be mistaken for completion. Fee earners still asking many basic questions have not yet made the new system routine, and withdrawing support now would stall the recovery.

questions.explanation: People move through a change in recognisable stages, and the support that helps at one stage is wasted or harmful at another. Read the stage from behaviour, especially the kind of questions people ask, then match the support to it: reasons early, listening during resistance, practical help during exploration, reinforcement once the new way is routine. Withdrawing support when results first improve is a common way to stall a change.
questions.mindset: Read where people are in a change from what they ask, and support that stage rather than the one you expected.

questions.stem: You are managing a project that replaces a university's key-and-logbook system with card-based access control across 40 buildings. Your change impact assessment and training plan cover academic and professional staff. A walk-round with the estates manager shows that out-of-hours cleaning and security are provided by two contracted firms, whose 70 staff collect keys from the porters' lodge every night and will have to work in a completely different way. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the university's contracts team to notify both firms formally about the new system so that the firms can prepare their own staff for it.
options.rationale: The candidate treats a change to people's work as a contractual notice. The firms do not know the new routines in enough detail to prepare anyone, so the largest impact in the project is left unassessed and unsupported.

options.text: Add the contracted staff to the change impact assessment, and plan their briefing and training through each firm's own site supervisor.
options.rationale: The contractors' routine changes more than almost anyone's, because nightly key collection disappears entirely. They belong in the same analysis as employees, and their own supervisors are the people who direct and brief them day to day.

options.text: Send the contracted staff the quick-reference guide from the employee training plan, and add them to the go-live communication plan so they receive it in time.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes the contractors' change is the same as the employees' and reaches for existing plan artefacts. A guide written for daytime staff with existing cards does not cover night-time access, alarm setting or the loss of the lodge, which are the contractors' actual changes.

options.text: Let the porters' lodge keep issuing keys to the contracted staff for the first term, so that their established night-time routine is not disrupted.
options.rationale: The candidate avoids the change rather than managing it. A key route kept open for one group tends to become permanent, undermines the security purpose of the project, and still leaves the eventual change unplanned.

questions.explanation: A change impact assessment is scoped by whose work changes, not by who is on the payroll. Contractors, agency workers and partner staff whose routines are altered are affected groups, and they need the same analysis and planned support, delivered through the people who direct their daily work. Finding a missed group is a reason to extend the assessment, not to give that group a lighter treatment.
questions.mindset: Map the impact of a change by whose work changes, not by whose name is on the payroll.

questions.stem: A builders' merchant has moved its accounts receivable team from an old ledger to a new finance system. The approved transition plan, which you manage, ends parallel running once four consecutive weekly reconciliations match. That happened in week 8. Supervisors asked for 'a few more weeks until everyone is comfortable', and at week 14 clerks are still keying every invoice into both systems. Nobody has reported a functional gap. What should you do?

options.text: Agree a further four weeks of parallel running with the supervisors, and end it once each of them confirms that their whole team feels ready.
options.rationale: The candidate makes the exit depend on a feeling that parallel running itself prevents. While the old ledger is there, confidence in the new one never has to form, so the extension is likely to be followed by another.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to decide whether parallel running should now end, given that the supervisors have formally asked for it to continue.
options.rationale: The candidate escalates a decision the approved plan has already made and delegated. Treating an agreed exit criterion as open to renegotiation on request weakens every other criterion in the plan.

options.text: Run refresher sessions on the new system for the clerks first, and set a date to end parallel running once those sessions have been completed.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes a skills gap that the evidence does not show: reconciliations match and nobody has reported a problem. Training does not remove the safety net, which is what keeps people keying twice.

options.text: Set a date now for switching off the old ledger, as the plan's exit criterion allows, and give the supervisors extra floor support for the final weeks.
options.rationale: The evidence the plan asked for has existed for six weeks and the double-keying is pure cost. Ending the fallback on a known date while adding support addresses the discomfort the supervisors describe without letting it keep the old system alive.

questions.explanation: Parallel running is a safety net with a purpose, and its exit criterion is what stops it becoming a permanent second system. Once the evidence the criterion asked for exists, confidence is built by removing the fallback with support in place, not by waiting for a comfort that the fallback itself prevents. An agreed exit condition is authority to act; re-opening it on request turns a transition into a habit.
questions.mindset: When the agreed exit criterion is met, remove the safety net and support people across the gap.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical wholesaler is moving three warehouses to a new picking process. The steering committee holds the go/no-go decision, and its approved readiness criteria require 90% of shift supervisors to be certified on the new exception-handling procedure. At the review in five days, every technical criterion is green, but certification stands at 68%, with the gap concentrated in one site's night shift. The sponsor reminds you that support for the old system ends in three weeks. What should you do?

options.text: Recommend that the committee declares a no-go because one of its agreed readiness criteria is unmet, and propose a revised go-live date once certification reaches 90%.
options.rationale: The candidate applies the criterion mechanically. The gap sits in one shift at one site and the old system's support is ending, so a blanket no-go may be the costliest option, and presenting only that one withholds choices the committee is entitled to weigh.

options.text: Arrange intensive certification sessions across all three sites over the next five days, aiming to close the gap before the committee meets.
options.rationale: The candidate tries to make the problem disappear before anyone sees it. Twenty-two points in five days, mostly on nights, is unlikely, and rushing certification turns a readiness measure into a box to tick.

options.text: Present the certification shortfall and where it sits, with options such as a staggered start for that night shift, so the committee decides against its own criteria.
options.rationale: The committee holds the decision and set the criterion, so it needs the real figure, its location and the realistic options. A localised gap may support a localised answer, but only the decision-maker can accept the residual risk.

options.text: Report overall readiness as amber, plan experienced floorwalkers for the affected night shift, and recommend going live on the scheduled date.
options.rationale: Floorwalkers may well be part of the answer, but the candidate blurs a criterion the committee set as a gate into a general amber. The people who own the risk should see the 68% figure and choose to accept it.

questions.explanation: Readiness criteria exist so that the body with go/no-go authority decides with the evidence in front of it. At a gate, the project manager shows exactly which criterion is short, where the gap sits and what the realistic responses are, rather than softening the status, substituting a personal verdict or racing to make the figure look met. A gap concentrated in one place often supports a targeted response, and choosing it belongs to whoever owns the risk.
questions.mindset: At a gate, give the decision-maker the real figure and the real options, then let them decide.

questions.stem: Your project gave a customs brokerage an automated declaration-checking tool. Adoption is at 92% and the project closes in four weeks. The business case's main benefit, cutting processing cost by €400,000 a year, depends on retiring the manual second check that the tool replaces. The operations manager, who owns the process after closure, wants to keep the manual check for six months 'to be safe'. The sponsor asks what should happen. What should you advise?

options.text: Ask the sponsor and the operations manager to agree evidence-based conditions and a date for retiring the manual check, and make them part of the closure handover.
options.rationale: Caution about removing a control in a regulated process is legitimate, and the decision is the process owner's. Turning 'to be safe' into agreed exit evidence and a date gives the benefit an owner and a route after the project has gone.

options.text: Extend the project by six months so that the project team itself can oversee retiring the manual check and confirm the annual saving before formal closure.
options.rationale: The candidate keeps a project open to carry out an operational decision that belongs to the business. It adds cost, delays the handover and still does not settle who decides when the check goes.

options.text: Retire the manual check four weeks after closure as the business case assumed, since the tool's accuracy has already been proven in testing.
options.rationale: The candidate overrides the process owner on a control they will be accountable for. Test accuracy is not live evidence, and a check removed against the owner's judgement is likely to reappear in another form.

options.text: Close the project on schedule, recording in the closure report that the annual saving is delayed and that the manual second check remains in place for now.
options.rationale: The candidate documents the problem instead of handing it over. With no conditions, date or owner attached, 'six months to be safe' tends to become permanent and the main benefit quietly disappears.

questions.explanation: The benefits of an organisational change usually arrive after the project has ended, so the project's last task is to leave each one with an owner, conditions and a date. Caution about retiring an old control belongs to whoever runs the process; the project's role is to turn that caution into explicit exit evidence that the owner and sponsor have agreed. A project that stays open to finish the job, or closes without that agreement, leaves the benefit with nobody.
questions.mindset: Hand over the unfinished part of a change with an owner, a condition and a date attached.

questions.stem: Your project has replaced paper near-miss forms with a mobile app for 300 technicians at an offshore wind maintenance contractor. Training went well and the app is quick to use, yet near-miss reports have fallen by a third. Technicians tell you privately that two colleagues were disciplined last year after reporting their own near misses. The sponsor proposes a monthly near-miss reporting target for every crew. What should the project manager recommend?

options.text: Add an anonymous reporting option to the app, so that technicians can log near misses without being identified to supervisors, managers or the safety team.
options.rationale: This is the most tempting alternative because it lowers the barrier quickly. But the candidate works around the fear rather than removing it: anonymity tells the workforce that being named is still dangerous and stops anyone following a report up.

options.text: Adopt the sponsor's crew targets for one quarter, but review the quality of reports alongside their volume so that trivial reports are screened out.
options.rationale: The candidate accepts the sponsor's premise and tries to manage its side effects. Under fear, a target buys safe and trivial reports; screening them out does not bring back the self-reports that matter.

options.text: Have supervisors record near misses on their crews' behalf at each end-of-shift debrief, so that no technician has to submit one in their own name.
options.rationale: The candidate shields individuals by routing reports through the hierarchy the technicians are wary of. Supervisors become a filter, and the reports least comfortable for management are the ones least likely to be written down.

options.text: Ask the operations director to state, in policy and in how the next reports are handled, that self-reported near misses will not lead to discipline.
options.rationale: The cause is what people believe happens to those who report, and that is set by how the organisation has treated reporters. Only the owner of the disciplinary practice can change it, and the next few cases are what will make the statement believable.

questions.explanation: A new tool cannot change what people believe happens to them when they use it. When reporting falls after a change, check what the culture rewards and punishes before adjusting the tool or adding targets: under fear, targets buy volume rather than candour, and workarounds that hide identity confirm the fear. The lever is the consequence itself, which sits with whoever owns the policy and is proved by how the next cases are handled.
questions.mindset: Before tuning the tool or the target, find out what people expect to happen to them if they comply.

questions.stem: Five months into an agile transformation in a parcel carrier's IT department, early enthusiasm is fading. Sceptical business managers say nothing has changed for them. The teams' own data shows that urgent depot fixes now reach production in four days instead of five weeks, but this appears only on team-level dashboards that business managers never open. What should the transformation lead do?

options.text: Show business managers the change in depot-fix lead time in their own terms, explaining what it has meant for the depots' daily work.
options.rationale: A five-week wait cut to four days is exactly the kind of win that answers 'nothing has changed', but only if it reaches the people saying it, in the language of their operations rather than the teams' dashboards.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to restate the long-term case for the transformation at the next all-staff briefing, reminding everyone why it began and what it is for.
options.rationale: The candidate answers a complaint about results with a restatement of intent. Sceptics who say nothing has changed are not short of a vision; they are short of evidence.

options.text: Bring in an external agile coach to run refresher workshops for the teams and their managers, rebuilding energy around the practices.
options.rationale: The candidate treats fading support as a practice problem inside the teams. The teams are already delivering; the gap is that the people judging the change cannot see what they have delivered.

options.text: Hold off reporting results until the transformation's first annual review, when the benefits can be shown with a full year of comparable data.
options.rationale: The candidate waits for perfect evidence while support drains away. Momentum is lost in months, and a credible early result shown now does more than a fuller one shown after sceptics have hardened.

questions.explanation: A change loses support when the people judging it cannot see its results, even when the results exist. Early, credible wins should be translated into outcomes that matter to sceptics and shown where those people already look, because momentum depends on evidence being visible as well as real. Restating the vision or retraining practitioners does not answer someone whose objection is that nothing has improved.
questions.mindset: Results that sceptics cannot see do not count in the argument for change.

questions.stem: A national charity is trialling agile ways of working before deciding whether to adopt them more widely. The sponsor wants the pilot to be the supporter-care team, which has the worst backlog, high staff turnover and a manager who openly doubts the approach, arguing that 'if it works there, it works anywhere'. Results are due to the board in six months. What should you, as the pilot lead, do?

options.text: Propose a team with a willing manager and a contained piece of work for the pilot, and plan for supporter care to follow in a later wave.
options.rationale: The pilot exists to find out whether the approach works and what it needs here. Conditions that let it be tested give the board a clear answer, and supporter care benefits more from joining once there is evidence and local experience.

options.text: Run the pilot in supporter care as the sponsor wants, setting modest targets for the board so that any measurable improvement counts as a success.
options.rationale: The candidate lowers the bar instead of fixing the design. With turnover and a doubting manager in the mix, the board will not learn whether agile works, and a weak result will be read as a verdict on the approach.

options.text: Run the pilot in supporter care, but first spend two months tackling its backlog and staffing gaps before introducing any agile practices.
options.rationale: The candidate spends a third of the pilot window on problems agile was never meant to fix, and keeps the doubting manager in charge of the trial. The board gets four months of thin evidence.

options.text: Run two pilots side by side, one in supporter care and one in a willing team, and compare the two sets of results for the board.
options.rationale: It looks rigorous, but the candidate doubles the coaching load and compares two contexts too different to isolate the approach. The struggling team's result is likely to dominate the board's reading.

questions.explanation: A pilot is an experiment whose purpose is to learn whether an approach works and what it needs, so its conditions should let the approach be tested rather than drowned out. Choosing the most troubled setting confounds the result with problems the approach was never meant to fix, and an early failure is read as a verdict on the change itself. Hard cases belong in later waves, once there is evidence and there are local advocates.
questions.mindset: Design a pilot to produce a clear answer, not to win an argument.

questions.stem: At a fashion e-commerce company, the chief executive launched the move to empowered product teams and talks about it at every town hall. Twice this month she has stopped a product owner in the corridor and asked for a feature to be built 'this sprint', and both times the team dropped committed work. Developers now joke that the real backlog is the chief executive's diary. As delivery lead, what should you do?

options.text: Coach the product owners to tell the chief executive, politely but firmly, that new requests go into the backlog for the next sprint planning.
options.rationale: The candidate puts the least powerful people in the situation into a contest of authority with the chief executive. Even if it works once, the signal her behaviour sends to everyone else is left untouched.

options.text: Raise both interruptions at the next transformation steering group, so the leadership team can agree a common rule for handling executive requests.
options.rationale: The candidate turns one leader's behaviour into a public policy debate in front of her peers. It is likely to embarrass the sponsor, make her defensive and delay the conversation that matters.

options.text: Meet the chief executive privately, show her the two interruptions and their effect on the teams, and offer her a regular slot in backlog refinement.
options.rationale: She is probably unaware that her shortcuts contradict her message. Private, specific feedback lets her see the cost without losing face, and a route into refinement meets her legitimate need to influence priorities in a way the new model supports.

options.text: Let the teams absorb the occasional executive request while protecting the rest of each sprint, since her continuing support for the change matters most.
options.rationale: The candidate protects the sponsor relationship at the cost of the change itself. Teams are reading what the chief executive does, and accepting the bypass confirms that empowerment stops at the top.

questions.explanation: People judge a change by what its leaders do, and one visible contradiction outweighs many speeches. When a sponsor's behaviour undermines the change, show them privately and with specifics what it is costing, and give their legitimate need a route that fits the new way of working. Leaving the contradiction alone, or confronting it in public, teaches the organisation that the change is optional at the top.
questions.mindset: Show leaders the effect of what they do, because the organisation watches that more than what they say.

questions.stem: A public broadcaster is retiring the scheduling tool one of its teams built and maintained for twelve years, and that team now works on the replacement. In planning sessions, members keep defending features of the old tool and arguing against design choices in the new one. The product owner wants to move two of them to other teams. They are the people who know the scheduling rules best. What should you, as the agile delivery lead, do?

options.text: Agree to the product owner's request and move the two most vocal members to other teams, replacing them with developers who have no attachment to the old tool.
options.rationale: The candidate removes the resistance along with the knowledge the replacement most needs. The rest of the team also learns that voicing a loss gets people moved, so the objections go quiet rather than away.

options.text: Mark the old tool's retirement with the team, recognising what it achieved, and ask them to identify which of its rules the replacement must carry over.
options.rationale: The arguments are mostly about losing something the team built and is proud of. Acknowledging that openly, and pointing their expertise at what must survive, turns the people defending the old tool into the ones who make the new one better.

options.text: Remind the team that the decision to retire the old tool is final, and ask them to keep planning discussions focused on the new product only.
options.rationale: The candidate treats grief as a discipline problem. Being told the decision is final does nothing for the sense of loss, which then resurfaces as quieter objections and slower work.

options.text: Give the team a dedicated backlog of improvements to the old tool for its remaining months, so their expertise stays engaged during the switch.
options.rationale: The candidate postpones the ending instead of acknowledging it. Splitting the team's attention prolongs the attachment and delays the moment they commit to the replacement.

questions.explanation: People resist an ending before they resist a new beginning, and what looks like opposition to a new design is often grief for something they built. Acknowledging the ending openly, and channelling the expertise behind the attachment into the new work, converts defenders into contributors. Removing them, overruling them or prolonging the old work all leave the loss unaddressed.
questions.mindset: Acknowledge what people are losing before asking them to commit to what replaces it.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is replacing a national museum group's finance system, and go-live is fixed for 1 March. HR's restructure of the finance function into new shared-service teams takes effect on 15 March, after a consultation process you do not control. The system's approval permissions have been built around the new teams, so staff would be trained on roles they will not hold for two weeks. You own the release plan. What should you do?

options.text: Ask HR to bring the restructure forward to 1 March so that the new roles and the new system start for everyone on the same day.
options.rationale: The candidate asks another function to move a date set by a consultation process the project does not control, and that HR may not be free to shorten, before using the flexibility inside the project's own plan.

options.text: Go live with permissions mapped to the current roles, and schedule a small release that switches them to the new team structure on 15 March.
options.rationale: It costs some extra configuration, but it keeps both fixed dates and lets people learn the system in the jobs they actually hold. The second step is small and lands on the day the new structure becomes real.

options.text: Move go-live to 15 March so that the system and the restructure take effect together and staff experience one change rather than two.
options.rationale: One date looks simpler, but the candidate stacks two disruptions on the same day and moves a date the stem says is fixed. Staff absorb a new team and a new system at once, with no settled ground under either.

options.text: Go live on 1 March with the new-team permissions, and have finance managers manually approve any transactions that fall outside them for two weeks.
options.rationale: The candidate keeps the design pure and pushes the mismatch onto people. Two weeks of manual workarounds in the first fortnight of a new system teaches staff that the system does not fit how they work.

questions.explanation: When a system change and an organisational change land close together, the system should fit the organisation people actually work in on the day they start using it. Where dates you do not own cannot move, an interim configuration that costs a little extra work is usually cheaper than training people on roles they do not hold or stacking two disruptions on one day. Use the flexibility in your own plan before asking others to move theirs.
questions.mindset: Fit the system to the organisation people work in today, and plan the step to tomorrow's.

questions.stem: Your agile team is about to release a knowledge base to the 220 agents at a telecoms support centre. The intent is that agents resolve more customer problems on first contact by using shared articles instead of escalating them. The head of support asks you to choose two measures to track from release onward that will show whether the change is genuinely being adopted. Which two measures should you choose?

options.text: The number of agents who log in to the knowledge base during each week after release
options.rationale: The candidate measures access rather than use. Agents can open the knowledge base to satisfy a manager and still resolve every problem the old way.

options.text: The proportion of resolved tickets that have a knowledge article linked to them
options.rationale: This sits inside the work itself: it shows how often an article was actually used to resolve a real customer problem, which is the behaviour the change asks for.

options.text: The percentage of agents who have completed the knowledge base training module
options.rationale: The candidate counts preparation, not change. Training completion says agents were shown the tool, not that their way of working has moved.

options.text: First-contact resolution rate for ticket types that have an article available
options.rationale: This ties adoption to the outcome the change was meant to produce. Restricting it to ticket types with articles keeps the measure about the knowledge base rather than about the whole support operation.

options.text: The number of new articles written and published by agents during each sprint
options.rationale: Contribution matters later, but the candidate measures production instead of use. A count of articles also invites short, thin entries written to move the number.

options.text: Agents' satisfaction with the knowledge base in a monthly pulse survey
options.rationale: The candidate takes sentiment for behaviour. Agents can like a tool and still not use it on live calls, and a survey cannot show whether problems were resolved.

questions.explanation: Adoption is a change in how work gets done, so its measures should sit inside the work and connect to the outcome the change was meant to produce. Activity measures such as logins, training completions and satisfaction are easy to collect and easy to satisfy without anything changing. Pair a behaviour measure with an outcome measure, and the pair shows both whether people are using the change and whether using it is paying off.
questions.mindset: Measure a change where the work happens, not where it is easiest to count.

questions.stem: A pensions administrator is moving from separate analysis, development and testing departments to cross-functional product teams. The test analysts, most with over a decade of service, are resisting. They say they will lose their professional standards, their career path and their collective voice, since each team will have one tester reporting to a product-focused team lead. Their department head supports the change. Which two actions should the transformation lead take?

options.text: Set up a testing community of practice that owns test standards across all teams, led by a senior test analyst.
options.rationale: It keeps the professional standards and the collective voice the analysts are afraid of losing, without pulling them back out of the product teams. A senior analyst leading it gives the craft a visible home.

options.text: Keep a central testing team for the first year and let product teams request testers from it as they need them.
options.rationale: The candidate resolves the resistance by keeping the structure the change exists to remove. Hand-offs between departments survive, and a year later the same conversation has to be had again.

options.text: Agree with HR a career framework for testers in the new teams, with senior grades that do not require moving into team leadership.
options.rationale: The fear about career paths is concrete and justified: if the only way up is a product team lead role, specialists have nowhere to progress. A specialist route answers that directly.

options.text: Reassure the test analysts that no jobs will be lost and that their current grades will be protected under the new structure.
options.rationale: The candidate answers a concern the analysts did not raise. Their objection is standards, progression and voice, and job security promises may not be the transformation lead's to make in any case.

options.text: Ask the department head to run a dedicated session with the test analysts explaining again why the organisation is making the change.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes the problem is understanding. The analysts know why the change is happening; what they object to is what they lose, and repeating the rationale tells them they have not been heard.

questions.explanation: Resistance to a structural change often names exactly what people will lose, and when the loss is real the response is to redesign rather than persuade. Professional identity, standards and progression can be preserved inside a new structure through communities of practice and specialist career routes, without retreating to the old structure. Answering a different concern from the one raised, or repeating the rationale, tells people they have not been listened to.
questions.mindset: When resistance names a real loss, design the loss out rather than argue it away.

questions.stem: After an energy supplier acquired a smaller rival, your hybrid project must move both customer service teams onto one complaints process within nine months. The acquirer's 300 agents follow detailed scripts and escalate most decisions; the rival's 80 agents resolve complaints themselves within a goodwill budget and achieve much higher customer satisfaction. The integration director's draft plan simply extends the acquirer's process to everyone. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Extend the acquirer's process to everyone as drafted, since it already covers most agents and can be rolled out within the nine months.
options.rationale: The candidate confuses the larger process with the better one. It discards the clearest evidence in the scenario, the rival's satisfaction results, and tells the acquired staff that what they did well does not count.

options.text: Compare both teams' practices against their results to identify what each does better, before the combined process design is fixed.
options.rationale: The two cultures produce measurably different outcomes, so the design should start from evidence about which practices drive them rather than from which company bought which.

options.text: Let each team keep its own complaints process on the shared system until the rest of the two businesses' integration is complete.
options.rationale: The candidate defers the decision the project exists to make. Two processes on one system harden into two cultures inside one company, and the eventual merge becomes harder, not easier.

options.text: Involve agents and team leaders from both companies in designing the combined process, and explain the reasons for what is kept from each.
options.rationale: People accept a combined process more readily when they helped shape it and can see why choices were made. Including both sides also stops the smaller group's expertise being lost in a design built by the larger.

options.text: Move a group of the rival's agents into the acquirer's teams straight away, so that the two working cultures start to blend naturally.
options.rationale: The candidate mixes the teams before deciding which practices to keep. A small group placed inside a much larger one usually conforms to the majority, so the rival's stronger practices are lost by default.

questions.explanation: In an integration, the culture behind each organisation's way of working is part of what was acquired, and the larger party's process is not automatically the better one. Compare practices against results before choosing, and build the combined design with people from both sides so that decisions are understood and owned. Integrations that skip this step tend to lose the smaller organisation's strengths along with its staff.
questions.mindset: Judge each side's way of working by its results, not by which side bought the other.

questions.stem: Each organisation below is planning how to move its people onto a new way of working. Match each situation to the deployment approach that best fits the cost of failure and the organisation's capacity to support the change. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A payroll change for 5,000 staff, where an error means people go unpaid and both systems can be run side by side for one monthly cycle.
A new stock-ordering process for 240 near-identical convenience stores, where the central support team can coach only about 20 stores through their first weeks at a time.
A new interest calculation that a regulator requires every branch of a bank to apply from the same date, where the old and new rules cannot coexist.
