options.text: Parallel running of the old and new arrangements
options.rationale: Where a failure is intolerable and both arrangements can run at once, running them side by side lets the new one be proved against the old before anyone depends on it.

options.text: Phased rollout in planned waves
options.rationale: The binding constraint is support capacity. Waves sized to what the support team can carry let each group of stores get real help in its first weeks, and later waves benefit from what earlier ones taught.

options.text: A single cutover for everyone on one date
options.rationale: When rules cannot coexist and a regulator fixes the date, staggering is not available. The work goes into preparation and readiness so that the one cutover is well supported.

options.text: A pilot at one site, then a pause to evaluate before deciding whether to continue
options.rationale: Not used. A pilot with an evaluation pause answers whether a change should proceed at all. In each situation above that decision is already made, and the question is how to roll it out.

questions.explanation: The deployment approach is chosen from two things: what a failure would cost, and how much change the organisation can support at once. Where failure is intolerable and running both is possible, run both; where support capacity is the limit, release in waves that capacity can carry; where rules cannot coexist, cut over once and prepare intensively. A pilot answers whether to proceed, which is a different question from how to roll out something already decided.
questions.mindset: Choose how to roll out a change from the cost of failure and the capacity to support it.

questions.stem: A hotel group's hybrid project is rolling out a new purchasing system in four releases over a year to 400 staff across its properties. Complete each sentence with the response that fits best. Two choices are not used.

prompts.text: Training for all 400 staff was planned as one block before the first release, although that release reaches only two pilot hotels and later releases will change the screens. The project manager should
The third release lets general managers approve purchases up to £5,000 instead of £1,000, but the group finance policy, owned by the finance director, still says £1,000. The project manager should

options.text: schedule training for each group shortly before it starts using the release it will work with
options.rationale: Skills taught months before they are used fade, and later releases would overtake them anyway. Training each group just ahead of its own first use means people learn the version they will actually meet.

options.text: ask the finance director to approve a revised policy that takes effect on the release date
options.rationale: The limit is written into a policy someone else owns. Aligning the policy change with the release means managers are never asked to choose between what the system allows and what the rulebook says.

options.text: keep the full training block up front so that every user is prepared before any release goes live
options.rationale: Not used. Front-loading suits a single cutover. Here most staff would wait months to use what they learned, and the screens they were trained on would change before they reached them.

options.text: configure the new limit and have the policy updated once the release has been in use for a quarter
options.rationale: Not used. Running the system ahead of the policy leaves managers approving purchases the policy forbids, and treats a rule owned by the finance director as something the project can update when convenient.

questions.explanation: In iterative delivery, the people side of the change has to be timed to the release that makes it real. Training delivered long before people use what they learned decays and is overtaken by later changes, so it belongs just ahead of each group's first use. Rules written into policy belong to their owner and should change at the moment the system starts enabling the new behaviour, or staff are left choosing between the tool and the rulebook.
questions.mindset: Time each part of the people change to the release that makes it real.

questions.stem: A utility's billing team of 60 advisers each handles 40 account queries a day. After the new billing system goes live, past experience suggests productivity will fall by 30% for the first 10 working days and by 15% for the next 20 working days. Agency advisers, each clearing 25 queries a day at £180 a day, will cover the shortfall. Work out the figures the transition budget needs.

blanks.label: Total queries the permanent team will not handle across the 30 working days
blanks.rationale: Normal capacity is 60 × 40 = 2,400 queries a day. The dip loses 2,400 × 0.30 × 10 = 7,200 in the first period and 2,400 × 0.15 × 20 = 7,200 in the second, a total of 14,400.

blanks.label: Agency adviser-days needed to clear that shortfall
blanks.rationale: Each agency adviser clears 25 queries a day, so 14,400 ÷ 25 = 576 adviser-days, roughly 19 agency staff across the 30 working days.

blanks.label: Agency cost to include in the transition budget, in £
blanks.rationale: 576 adviser-days × £180 = £103,680. This is the cost of the productivity dip itself, separate from training and the system.

questions.explanation: The dip in performance after a change has a cost, and a transition budget that leaves it out quietly assumes it will be absorbed by goodwill or a growing backlog. Convert the expected dip into lost output, then into the resources needed to cover it, so the sponsor sees the cost of the transition alongside the cost of the system and can decide how much to fund. Putting a number on it also sets the expectation that performance falls before it rises.
questions.mindset: Put a number on the productivity dip, because an unfunded dip becomes a backlog and a complaint.

questions.stem: You are planning change support for an airport ground-handling company's move to electronic rostering. The diagram places each staff group by how much the change alters their work (impact) and by its score in last month's readiness assessment, with headcount shown. Your one experienced change coach is available for six weeks before go-live. Select the group she should work with first.

graphic.title: Staff groups plotted by impact of the change against readiness
graphic.caption: Select a staff group. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between groups, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Night-shift ramp agents — impact high, readiness low, 140 staff
regions.rationale: This group has the widest gap between what the change demands and what it is ready for: its work changes most and its readiness is lowest. Scarce coaching does the most good here.

regions.label: Rostering coordinators — impact high, readiness high, 10 staff
regions.rationale: Their work changes a great deal, which draws the eye, but they are already ready for it. The candidate weighs impact alone and spends the coach where the gap is smallest.

regions.label: Day-shift ramp agents — impact medium, readiness medium, 320 staff
regions.rationale: The candidate is drawn by headcount. A large group with a moderate change and moderate readiness has a smaller gap per person, and is easier to reach through ordinary briefings and training.

regions.label: Check-in agents — impact medium, readiness high, 90 staff
regions.rationale: A moderate change for a group already prepared for it is the case least in need of a specialist. The candidate would be spending scarce support on reassurance rather than on a real gap.

regions.label: Duty managers — impact low, readiness low, 25 staff
regions.rationale: The candidate is drawn by the lowest readiness score, but the change barely touches this group's work. Low readiness matters in proportion to how much the change asks of people.

questions.explanation: Change support is a scarce resource, and it does most good where the change is large and readiness is low, because that is where the gap between what the change demands and what people can manage is widest. Group size, impact alone and low readiness alone are each tempting signals, but none of them measures the gap. Read impact and readiness together before allocating help, and reach the remaining groups through lighter, wider channels.
questions.mindset: Send scarce change support to where the change is biggest and readiness is lowest.
